synopsis: ISO 16001:2017, dated November 2017 and confirmed in 2023, sets performance and test requirements for object-detection systems and visibility aids; its scope is warning and visibility, not braking [f6744, f2181]. The booklet identifies it as the only off-road standard found with hard detection and warning numbers, reporting a maximum detection time of 300 ms, audible warnings at least 3 dB above ambient, and a flashing red light for the most severe warning [f160, f2065, f2066]. It also reports continuous self-checking and no single-action disablement, while noting that the 2017 edition has no dedicated lidar annex [f2067, f2068, f12614]. ISO 5006 and ISO 16001 visibility-type methods support geometric computation of coverage and blind zones for each machine model before hardware arrives, although ISO 5006 was not verified in the research [f5602, f11549, f2197]. ISO 16001 defines a test body, detection zone and detection time, and specifies physical-test-body procedures; evidence that it accepts simulation was not found, and it does not set statistical sample sizes or simulation-credibility rules [f5354, f11232, f11192, f6749]. Although the 300 ms limit is attributed to public-preview clause 4.5 and used in physics parameterisation, it was not verified against the purchased standard and should be confirmed before safety-case reliance [f7493, f7494, f7495].

relations.note: Both identify the only off-road standard found with hard detection and warning numbers.
Both distinguish warning coverage from braking coverage.
Duplicate definitions of test body, detection zone and detection time.
Both prohibit disabling the warning with a single action.
Duplicate glossary statements of the 300 ms detection limit.
Both report missing evidence of simulation acceptance for ISO 16001 and ISO 21815.
The annex inventory details the glossary's missing-lidar-annex finding.
Adds per-model geometry and computation before hardware arrival to the geometric-method example.
Specifies that the testing framework uses a physical test body.
Operationalises detection time and distinguishes it from operator-interface warning latency.
Public-preview clause supplies the 300 ms cap used in the detection-distance model.
Missing full-standard verification motivates confirmation before safety-case use.
Categorical requirement attribution is qualified by lack of full-standard verification.
Unverified ISO 5006 evidence qualifies reliance on its proposed geometric methods.
Mature surveyed-target testing supports prioritising directly relevant off-road standards over passenger-car protocols.
